blocks.content: Every Japanese verb belongs to one of three groups. The group determines *every* conjugation rule — get it right and the rest is predictable.

items: **Group 1 — Godan (五段):** ends in any う-column sound — く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, う, or る*. The stem changes shape across forms following phonetic patterns.
**Group 2 — Ichidan (一段):** ends in る, with an い or え vowel immediately before it. The stem never changes — you only remove the る.
**Group 3 — Irregular:** only する (to do) and くる (to come). Both must be memorised.

blocks.content: る-ending Group 1 verbs look identical to Group 2 in dictionary form. 帰る (kaeru), 走る (hashiru), 知る (shiru), 切る (kiru) are all Group 1. There is no reliable visual test — when in doubt, check a dictionary. Recognition comes with exposure.

The **ます form** is how you speak politely. It is the default for conversations with people you do not know well, in formal situations, and in service environments. It covers both present habit and future intention — Japanese does not separate these two ideas.
Formation

lines: Group 1: change the final u-vowel to i-vowel + ます
書く  → 書き + ます  → 書きます
話す  → 話し + ます  → 話します
待つ  → 待ち + ます  → 待ちます
Group 2: remove る + ます
食べる → 食べ + ます → 食べます
見る   → 見 + ます   → 見ます
Group 3:
する → します
来る → 来ます (きます)
Negative: replace ます with ません

rows.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。

blocks.content: ます covers both habits and planned future actions. Context makes the meaning clear — Japanese has no separate future tense.

ます is polite but not formal. Use it with a shop clerk, a new acquaintance, or a teacher. Among close friends, speakers drop to the plain (dictionary) form. Both are grammatically correct — register determines which fits.
The past tense is formed by replacing **ます** with **ました**. The negative past uses **ませんでした**. Both follow the same stem rules as the present tense — there is nothing new to memorise for the stem.

lines: Affirmative past: [stem] + ました
Negative past:    [stem] + ませんでした

rows.japanese: 朝ごはんを食べませんでした。
先週、東京に行きました。
rows.english: I went to Tokyo last week.

rows.japanese: レポートを書きませんでした。

blocks.content: Japanese past tense is clean — no distinction between simple past ("I ate") and perfect ("I have eaten") in the polite form. Time words and context carry that distinction.

Both **へ** and **に** can mark a destination when paired with a movement verb. They are often interchangeable, but each has a different focus: へ points at the direction of travel, に points at the arrival point. In everyday speech, に is more common.

lines: [Place] へ + [movement verb]   ← focus on the direction, the journey
[Place] に + [movement verb]   ← focus on the destination, arrival

rows.japanese: 駅のほうへ歩きました。
日本に引っ越しました。

blocks.content: に is required — not interchangeable with へ — with arrival verbs like 着く (to arrive) and 帰る (to return). These verbs already imply reaching a point, so に locks in the destination. 家に帰る = arrive back home. 家へ帰る = head toward home.
**で** marks *where an action takes place* — the venue or instrument of an activity. This is different from に, which marks *where something exists*. The verb is what tells you which particle to use.

lines: [Place] で + [action verb]   ← an action happens here
[Place] に + [existence verb] ← something exists here (います / あります)

rows.english: I read books on the train.

rows.japanese: 日本語で話してください。

left.label: で — action
left.description: Where something happens. Use with action verbs — running, studying, eating.

right.label: に — existence
right.description: Where something is. Use with います and あります — existing, being.

blocks.content: で vs に for location is one of the most common early errors. The verb tells you which to use: action verbs → で, existence verbs (います/あります) → に.

lessons.title: いる and ある — Existence

blocks.content: Japanese uses two different verbs to express "there is" or "to be," and the choice depends entirely on what kind of thing exists. **いる** is for living things. **ある** is for everything else.

lines: [Living thing] が [Place] に います   → there is/are (animate)
[Object/thing] が [Place] に あります  → there is/are (inanimate)

left.label: います
left.description: People, animals — anything that moves under its own power.
left.example_en: There is a cat in the room.

right.label: あります
right.description: Objects, plants, buildings, and even scheduled events like meetings.
right.example_jp: 本が机の上にあります。
right.example_en: There is a book on the desk.

rows.japanese: 駅の前に銀行があります。
rows.romaji: Eki no mae ni ginkō ga arimasu.
rows.english: There's a bank in front of the station.

rows.japanese: 財布がバッグの中にあります。
rows.romaji: Saifu ga baggu no naka ni arimasu.
rows.english: My wallet is inside the bag.

blocks.content: あります is used for scheduled events too — 会議があります (there's a meeting), 授業があります (there's a class). Events are treated as inanimate things that exist on the calendar.
Using ある for people — 友達が外にある — sounds wrong at best and rude at worst. The animate/inanimate distinction is instinctive for native speakers.
Japanese numbers are straightforward up to 10,000. The same digits combine and stack to form larger values — 十一 is 10+1, 百二十三 is 100+20+3. Learn the base set and the rest follows.
4 (し) and 9 (く) are avoided in some contexts — し sounds like 死 (death) and く like 苦 (suffering). Hospital rooms sometimes skip these numbers. This is cultural awareness, not grammar.
Japanese does not use bare numbers to count objects. Numbers pair with **counters** — suffixes that classify what is being counted. The number reading also changes depending on which counter follows.

lines: [Number] + [Counter]
三人 (sannin)   — three people
二枚 (nimai)    — two sheets
一杯 (ippai)    — one cup

rows.japanese: りんごを二個買いました。

rows.english: Please give me one sheet of paper.

rows.japanese: コーヒーを一杯飲みました。
rows.english: I drank one cup of coffee.

rows.japanese: 車を二台持っています。

blocks.content: Number + counter combinations trigger phonetic changes. 一本 (ippon), 三本 (sanbon), 六本 (roppon) — the pattern follows Japanese sound rules. Don't try to memorise all variants at once. Learn the counter first and pick up the sound changes through exposure.

lessons.title: Asking How Many — いくつ / 何～

blocks.content: There are two ways to ask "how many" in Japanese. Use **いくつ** when the category is unspecified or you want a general count. Use **何** (なん) directly before the counter when the category is already known.

left.label: いくつ
left.description: General count — used when the category is unspecified, or for things without a fixed counter.
left.example_jp: りんごがいくつありますか。

right.label: 何 + counter
right.description: Category-specific — attach 何 (nan) directly before the counter you would normally use.

rows.english: How many books did you read?

blocks.content: いくつ is also used informally to ask someone's age — お子さんはいくつですか (How old is your child?). The direct "how old" question is 何歳 (nansai).
